utility.notes: NES is a municipally-owned utility and a local power company (distributor) for the Tennessee Valley Authority (TVA) — TVA generates and transmits power wholesale, while NES handles local distribution, billing, and customer-facing programs. Confirmed directly by the City's own permit page, which requires separate NES approval alongside the Metro Codes permit.

value.name: Tennessee Valley Authority (TVA)
value.notes: TVA is the wholesale power generator/transmitter for the entire region; NES is the local distribution utility purchasing from TVA and reselling to Nashville-area customers. This two-tier structure (a federal wholesale generator plus a locally-owned distributor) is structurally distinct from the single investor-owned or municipal utilities researched in most other states this session.

county.notes: Nashville and Davidson County operate a consolidated Metropolitan Government (Metro Nashville); the Metropolitan Department of Codes and Building Safety is the single permitting authority for the whole consolidated jurisdiction.

permit_authority.value: Metropolitan Department of Codes and Building Safety
permit_authority.notes: Tennessee's statewide code framework applies through the state Fire Marshal's office and local adoption, but enforcement is local. Metro Nashville-Davidson County's own Department of Codes and Building Safety is a genuinely consolidated authority for the whole city-county jurisdiction — the same efficient pattern as Louisville, KY and Indianapolis, IN researched earlier this session.

interconnection_url.notes: As a TVA local power company, NES does NOT offer traditional retail-rate net metering. Per NES's own 'NESolar Connect and NESolar Savings Guidelines' (effective October 2024), these two formal power-purchase programs are structured for LARGER systems, not typical single-family rooftop installations: NESolar Connect requires a minimum 200kW nameplate for solar facilities (35MW total program cap), and NESolar Savings covers systems up to 250kW DC with a minimum 50kWh average monthly excess generation (10MW total program cap) — both paid at fixed seasonal per-kWh rates (e.g., NESolar Savings: $0.03069/kWh summer, $0.03197/kWh winter) rather than retail-rate credit. For genuinely small residential systems below these thresholds, NES instead participates in TVA's separate 'Dispersed Power Production Program,' a net-billing mechanism with its own (lower) compensation rate — its exact residential rate was not independently confirmed from a primary TVA/NES source this session, so it is not stated here as a specific figure.

battery_programs.notes: NES's NESolar Savings program guidelines do permit 'solar PV with battery storage' installations under that program's framework, but this describes program eligibility for larger systems, not a dedicated residential battery financial incentive, which was not independently confirmed this session.

required_documents.notes: Per the City's own permit page. The permit application must be submitted by a licensed and experienced electrical contractor registered with Metro Codes' Building Safety Administration. NES's own interconnection process runs in parallel and separately requires a 'Nashville Electric Service Application for Interconnection of Renewable Generation form' no later than 60 days before power production begins.

value.notes: Per the City's own page: residential permits typically receive approval within one week, with a standard target of 30 days for completed applications; commercial projects may require extended review. Permits remain valid for 6 months from issuance; work must commence and progress continuously or the permit becomes invalid.

other_conditions: The permit application and the NES interconnection application run in parallel and both must be completed before the system can be energized
